newsitem.title: UK: UK manufacturing output falls as pound rises.
newsitem.headline: UK manufacturing output falls as pound rises.

text.p: British manufacturing output dipped in March, official figures showed on Wednesday, increasing fears that the pound's rise is punishing industries which have barely made it out of recession.
The Office for National Statistics said manufacturing output fell by 0.1 percent in March compared with a 0.2 percent rise in February.
That fall comes against a background of widespread industrial weakness in Britain. In the year to March, manufacturing output rose by only 1.4 percent, down from 1.7 percent in the year to February.
The government made no new comment on the figures. But on Tuesday Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, who already had the data, said the level of manufacturing activity was disappointing.
Overall industrial production, which includes manufacturing and energy industry output, also dropped 0.1 percent in March as warmer weather cut demand for gas and electricity.
City economists said Brown's move to put up interest rates by a quarter point to 6.25 percent on Tuesday would probably hurt the industrial sector even more by propelling the pound even higher.

"These figures serve as a timely reminder that industry needs more rises in interest rates -- and the further rise in the pound they could prompt -- like a hole in the head," said Jonathan Loynes, U.K. economist at HSBC Markets.

The pound gained three pfennigs on Tuesday after the rate rise, which accompanied sweeping changes to the Bank of England with Brown giving the central bank operational control over interest rates. For manufacturers the more the pound rises, the more expensive their exports become.

Experts said that the newly-empowered cental bank already appeared keen for interest rates to go even higher to dampen inflationary pressures. But the weakness in industry might make the new monetary policy committee hold back for a while.

"While base rates will probably head higher between now and the end of the year, the new monetary policy committee should find this evidence persuasive enough to recommend that base rates remain on hold for the time being," said Andrew Cates, U.K. economist at UBS.

The pound has soared by about 19 percent on a trade-weighted since last August. Manufacturers have complained bitterly since the beginning of the year that the strong currency has sapped demand for British goods abroad and business surveys show export orders have fallen sharply.
The ONS said there was no sign as yet that the stronger currency was affecting exports. "Output in exports sectors are holding up well, particularly chemicals and engineering," said one statistician.

But Cates said the new Bank committee, due to meet for the first time in June, should at least wait until Brown's forthcoming mini-budget before raising rates again, and possibly fuelling another surge in the pound.
Brown plans to present the mini-budget in the next two months. Expectations are growing that it will raise personal taxes to rein in booming high street spending.

Brown has already promised one tax cut and one tax rise. He said he will lower the level of indirect tax on heating fuel from to five percent from eight percent, and levy a windfall tax on the profits of privatised utilities. But economists said it is households, not companies, that need to be taxed.
Labour is committed not to raise the level of income tax, but economists said he could tighten personal allowances and cut or abolish tax relief on home loan repayments.
